[39m [38;5;143m+ 63 ## Strategies for Long-Running and Multi-Tasking Workflows
[39m [38;5;143m+ 64
[39m [38;5;143m+ 65 The schedule tool becomes much more powerful when combined with `bash`. Instead   
[39m [38;5;143mof blocking on a long command or busy-waiting in a loop, use these patterns to work    
[39m [38;5;143masynchronously.
[39m [38;5;143m+ 66
[39m [38;5;143m+ 67 ### Strategy 1: Fire and Check (Basic Loop)
[39m [38;5;143m+ 68
[39m [38;5;143m+ 69 The simplest pattern. Kick off a long command, set a timer, walk away.
[39m [38;5;143m+ 70
[39m [38;5;143m+ 71 ```
[39m [38;5;143m+ 72 # Agent turn 1
[39m [38;5;143m+ 73 bash(ia upload bigfile.tar.gz)
[39m [38;5;143m+ 74 schedule(duration: "30s", note: "check if ia upload finished")
[39m [38;5;143m+ 75 # End turn → timer fires → agent comes back
[39m [38;5;143m+ 76 ```
[39m [38;5;143m+ 77
[39m [38;5;143m+ 78 **Best for:** Single long-running commands where you don't know exact runtime.    
[39m [38;5;143m+ 79
[39m [38;5;143m+ 80 ### Strategy 2: Staggered Timers (Parallel Work)
[39m [38;5;143m+ 81
[39m [38;5;143m+ 82 Fire multiple independent commands at once, each with its own timer. They come    
[39m [38;5;143mback as they finish, no need to batch.
[39m [38;5;143m+ 83
[39m [38;5;143m+ 84 ```
[39m [38;5;143m+ 85 # Agent turn 1 — fire all three, set staggered checks
[39m [38;5;143m+ 86 bash(pnpm build:images)
[39m [38;5;143m+ 87 schedule(duration: "30s", note: "check images build")
[39m [38;5;143m+ 88
[39m [38;5;143m+ 89 bash(ia upload release-01.zip)
[39m [38;5;143m+ 90 schedule(duration: "2m", note: "check release-01 upload")
[39m [38;5;143m+ 91
[39m [38;5;143m+ 92 bash(pnpm run graph-data)
[39m [38;5;143m+ 93 schedule(duration: "1m", note: "check graph-data generation")
[39m [38;5;143m+ 94 # End turn — each timer independently fires the agent
[39m [38;5;143m+ 95 ```
[39m [38;5;143m+ 96
[39m [38;5;143m+ 97 **Best for:** Independent tasks with different expected runtimes. Avoids waiting  
[39m [38;5;143mfor the slowest task just to check on a fast one.
[39m [38;5;143m+ 98
[39m [38;5;143m+ 99 ### Strategy 3: Daisy Chain (Conditional Pipeline)
[39m [38;5;143m+100
[39m [38;5;143m+101 Chain commands conditionally — the result of one determines what runs next.       
[39m [38;5;143m+102
[39m [38;5;143m+103 ```
[39m [38;5;143m+104 # Agent turn 1
[39m [38;5;143m+105 bash(pnpm run validate-content)
[39m [38;5;143m+106 schedule(duration: "15s", note: "check content validation")
[39m [38;5;143m+107 # Timer fires — if validation passed, fire the build
[39m [38;5;143m+108 # Agent turn 2
[39m [38;5;143m+109 bash(pnpm build)
[39m [38;5;143m+110 schedule(duration: "2m", note: "check build")
[39m [38;5;143m+111 ```
[39m [38;5;143m+112
[39m [38;5;143m+113 **Best for:** Pipelines where each step depends on the previous one succeeding.   
[39m [38;5;143m+114
[39m [38;5;143m+115 ### Strategy 4: Batched Checkpoint (One Timer, Many Commands)
[39m [38;5;143m+116
[39m [38;5;143m+117 Fire several commands, set one timer for the longest expected runtime, check      
[39m [38;5;143meverything at once.
[39m [38;5;143m+118
[39m [38;5;143m+119 ```
[39m [38;5;143m+120 # Agent turn 1 — fire all parallel tasks
[39m [38;5;143m+121 bash(ia upload images.zip)
[39m [38;5;143m+122 b ash(ia upload documents.zip)
[39m [38;5;143m+123 b ash(ia upload videos.zip)

[39m [38;5;143m+125 # End turn — single timer fires, check all three at once
[39m [38;5;143m+126 ```
[39m [38;5;143m+127
[39m [38;5;143m+128 **Best for:** Tasks with similar expected runtimes. Simpler to manage than        
[39m [38;5;143mstaggered timers when timing is predictable.
[39m [38;5;143m+129
[39m [38;5;143m+130 ### Strategy 5: Progressive Polling with Dignity
[39m [38;5;143m+131
[39m [38;5;143m+132 Instead of fixed 30s loops, scale the interval up. Start aggressive, back off as  
[39m [38;5;143mthe task runs longer.
[39m [38;5;143m+133
[39m [38;5;143m+134 ```
[39m [38;5;143m+135 # Agent turn 1

[39m [38;5;143m+139 # Timer fires — still running
[39m [38;5;143m+140 # Agent turn 2
[39m [38;5;143m+141 schedule(duration: "1m", note: "check build (second check)")
[39m [38;5;143m+142
[39m [38;5;143m+143 # Timer fires — still running
[39m [38;5;143m+144 # Agent turn 3
[39m [38;5;143m+145 schedule(duration: "2m", note: "check build (third check)")
[39m [38;5;143m+146 ```
[39m [38;5;143m+147

[39m [38;5;143m+149
[39m [38;5;143m+150 ### Strategy 6: Error Pre-Flight

[39m [38;5;143m+152 Run a quick validation first. Only fire the long command if the pre-flight        
[39m [38;5;143mpasses. Saves time and timer slots.

[39m [38;5;143m+154 ```

[39m [38;5;143m+46 The **schedule tool** is a Pi-exclusive feature that enables async workflows. Pi   
[39m [38;5;143mcan fire off a long-running bash command, set a timer, end its turn, and come back     
[39m [38;5;143mwhen the timer fires — no busy-waiting or polling loops needed.
[39m [38;5;143m+47
[39m [38;5;143m+48 **How Pi uses it:**
[39m [38;5;143m+49
[39m [38;5;143m+50 1. Pi runs a long command with `bash` (e.g., `ia upload`, `pnpm build`).
[39m [38;5;143m+51 2. Pi calls `schedule(duration, note)` — sets a timer for N seconds/minutes.       
[39m [38;5;143m+52 3. Pi ends its turn. Timer runs in the background.
[39m [38;5;143m+53 4. Timer fires — Pi gets pinged with the note it left itself and picks up where it 
[39m [38;5;143mleft off.
[39m [38;5;143m+54
[39m [38;5;143m+55 **Why it matters for this vault:** Large operations like uploading Internet        
[39m [38;5;143mArchive items, generating graph data, or running site builds can take minutes. With    
[39m [38;5;143mthe schedule tool, Pi can kick these off and do other work (or wait quietly) instead   
[39m [38;5;143mof blocking.
